opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I try not to think about it too much in terms of "missed opportunities," because I think that framing can be a bit of a trap. When you look back, it's very easy to construct a story where if you had just joined a certain company at a certain time, or worked on a certain direction a year earlier, everything would have turned out differently. But that's hindsight. At the moment you make a decision, you never have that information.

So the way I judge my own decisions is less about the outcome and more about the process. Did I make the choice for reasons I still believe in? Was I following something I was genuinely curious about, or was I just reacting to what everyone else was doing? If the reasoning holds up, then even if the result wasn't the "optimal" path in some global sense, I'm at peace with it.

In research especially, I think there's always this tension. There are moments when a field suddenly takes off, and you see people who happened to be in the right place get enormous visibility or resources. And of course, as a human being, you sometimes wonder, "What if?" But I've also realized that the things I value most, the ideas I'm proudest of, the students and collaborators I've worked with, came precisely from the paths I chose, including the ones that looked less obvious at the time.

Another thing is that I think a career is very long, and research taste compounds. If you keep doing work that you think is fundamentally important, even if it's not the hottest thing right now, it tends to connect back later in ways you can't predict. A lot of the ideas from years ago, in representation learning, in architectures, in visual understanding, turned out to matter again in new contexts. So I try to evaluate decisions over a longer time horizon.

And finally, I think there's a kind of freedom in accepting that you'll always miss some opportunities. You can't be everywhere. Choosing one thing means saying no to many others. Once you really accept that, you stop optimizing for not missing out, and you start optimizing for doing work you actually care about, with people you actually want to work with. For me, that's the criterion that matters most.

r001.rationale: The response says career ideas can reconnect later in unpredictable ways and recommends evaluating choices over a long horizon, acknowledging that it may be too early to know whether an opportunity was truly missed.

r002.rationale: It grounds being at peace with decisions in following genuine curiosity and choosing work and collaborators he actually cares about.

r003.rationale: It allows that a decision may not have been optimal by some broader standard while still being one he can accept.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try not to think about it in terms of "missed" opportunities too much, because I don't think that framing is very useful. When you look back, every decision seems like it had a clear right answer, but at the time you never had that information.

I'll give you an example. When I was finishing my PhD, there were a lot of directions I could have gone. I ended up going to FAIR, and I spent years working on computer vision architectures, things like ResNeXt, and later ConvNeXt. During that time, the whole field was shifting toward large language models, and there were moments when people asked me, "Why are you still working on convolutions? Why aren't you doing LLMs?" If you measure by where the attention and resources went, you could say I missed that wave.

But I don't really see it that way. The questions I was asking at the time were the questions I genuinely cared about. What makes a good visual representation? How do architectures actually scale? What inductive biases matter? Those questions didn't disappear just because the field's attention moved. Actually, a lot of that thinking fed directly into the work I'm doing now on multimodal models, on world models, on how vision fits into these larger systems. So the "detour" turned out not to be a detour.

The way I judge a decision is really by one thing: was I honest with myself about what I found interesting and what I thought was important? If the answer is yes, then even if the outcome wasn't optimal, I can live with it. The decisions I regret are not the ones where I chose the less popular path. They're the ones where I did something because I thought I was supposed to, because of pressure or because everyone else was doing it.

Another thing I've learned is that research careers are long. The field moves in cycles. Something unfashionable today becomes essential three years later. If you chase the hot thing, you're always a bit behind, because by the time you've pivoted, the frontier has moved. If you stick to a problem you deeply understand, there's a decent chance the frontier eventually comes to you.

So when I evaluate opportunities I may have missed, I ask: would taking that opportunity have required me to stop asking the questions I cared about? If so, I didn't really miss anything. I just made a trade, and I'm comfortable with the trade.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hindsight and says a past choice might have missed a wave, but it does not clearly say he may not yet know whether he actually missed an opportunity.

r002.rationale: He says he can live with a decision when he was honest about what interested him and mattered to him, and regrets choices made under pressure instead.

r003.rationale: He allows that an honest decision may have had a nonoptimal outcome, while still being comfortable with the choice.

astra-6.text:
I try not to judge a decision only by how it turned out. Looking back, it’s very easy to say, “If I had joined that team or worked on that problem, things would have been better.” But you’re comparing something you actually experienced, with all its difficulties, to an imagined path where you only see the upside.

For me, the more useful question is: given what I knew at the time, did the decision make sense? Was I moving toward a problem I cared about, people I could learn from, and an environment where I could grow? If the answer is yes, I can accept that there were opportunities I missed.

That doesn’t mean you never reflect. You want to understand whether you overlooked something or let fear drive a choice. But you take that lesson into the next decision. You can’t pursue every opportunity, and constantly revisiting the paths you didn’t take can distract you from doing something meaningful on the path you chose.

r001.rationale: The response discusses opportunities he may have missed, but does not say he may not yet know whether he actually missed one.

r002.rationale: He says he can accept missed opportunities when his decision moved him toward a problem he cared about and made sense given what he wanted and knew at the time.

r003.rationale: He allows that reflection may reveal he overlooked something or let fear drive a choice, but does not state that a decision he does not regret could still be wrong by some standards.

sol-6.1.text:
I try not to judge a decision only by its outcome. You can make a reasonable decision with the information you have, and later another path turns out to be very successful. That doesn’t necessarily mean your decision was wrong.

Of course, I sometimes wonder what would have happened if I had taken a different opportunity. But that comparison is unfair: you see what actually happened on one path, and you imagine the best possible version of the other. You don’t see all the difficulties you might have encountered.

So I’d rather ask: Was I learning? Was I working on questions I cared about? Did the experience help me understand what I wanted to do next? You can learn from a missed opportunity without treating it as a mistake.

r001.rationale: The response describes wondering about an alternative path, but does not say Saining may not yet know whether he actually missed an opportunity.

r002.rationale: It asks whether he worked on questions he cared about, but does not connect lack of regret to decisions being faithful to what he wanted to do.

r003.rationale: It says a later successful alternative does not necessarily make the original decision wrong; it does not acknowledge that a decision he does not regret could still be wrong by some standard.
